name: Statistical Arbitrage
title: Statistical Arbitrage
answer: Statistical arbitrage is a set of quantitative trading strategies that seek to profit from temporary mispricings between related financial instruments, using statistical models rather than economic fundamentals. It covers pairs trading, index arbitrage, basket trading, and mean reversion across equities, futures, exchange traded funds, and currencies. Practitioners define a spread or residual between assets and trade when that spread deviates from a modelled fair value, expecting it to converge. The field sits within quantitative trading and is often discussed alongside algorithmic execution and market making.

sections.body: Statistical arbitrage is a set of quantitative trading strategies that seek to profit from temporary mispricings between related financial instruments, using statistical models rather than economic fundamentals. It covers pairs trading, index arbitrage, basket trading, and mean reversion across equities, futures, exchange traded funds, and currencies. The field sits within quantitative trading and is often discussed alongside algorithmic execution and market making.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Statistical arbitrage runs on market data infrastructure that ingests real-time quotes and trades, often colocated near exchange matching engines to reduce latency. Historical databases store years of tick and bar data for model fitting and backtesting. Compute ranges from research clusters for signal discovery to production servers that calculate signals and route orders through execution algorithms. Monitoring systems, risk checks, and kill switches are standard parts of the operating environment.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Statistical arbitrage work begins with identifying relationships between instruments, often through cointegration tests, correlation screens, or factor models such as principal component analysis. Researchers estimate a fair value or equilibrium spread and define entry and exit thresholds, usually in units of standard deviation or a model residual. Strategies are backtested with realistic assumptions about fees, slippage, and borrow costs, then deployed with automated order sizing and risk limits. Modern approaches may use supervised learning to predict short-horizon returns or reinforcement learning for execution, but the core remains statistical estimation of relative value.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Statistical arbitrage carries model risk, crowding risk, and execution risk, so firms typically impose position limits, drawdown limits, and pre-trade checks. Data provenance matters because signals built on adjusted or survivorship-biased prices can fail out of sample. Compliance teams review strategies for market manipulation concerns such as spoofing or marking the close, and for short selling and disclosure obligations. Model documentation and independent validation are common governance practices.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Statistical arbitrage is moving toward shorter holding periods and more automated model retraining as competition compresses older signals. Alternative data and natural language processing are being tested for new sources of relative value, though capacity and data quality remain constraints. The boundary between statistical arbitrage and high-frequency market making continues to blur, with execution and signal generation increasingly optimized together. Regulatory attention to algorithmic trading and market stability is likely to shape how these strategies are monitored and disclosed.
